The reasoning process follows a hierarchical structure: early layers identify entities, middle layers interpret actions, and final layers synthesize information.
Self-influence scores show how token importance changes across layers, revealing the reasoning path.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was conducted primarily on the GPT-2 model and may not generalize to larger or different architectures without adaptation.
Calculating self-influence requires computationally intensive methods, which may pose scalability challenges for more complex models.
Our work focused on a single task (Indirect Object Identification, or IOI), and the applicability of these findings to other natural language processing tasks remains an open question.
future_direction: Explore the adaptability of this approach across varied tasks and model architectures
Investigate methods to optimize computational efficiency
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved significant success; however, their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque due to the complexity of non-linear interactions and high-dimensional operations. While previous studies have demonstrated that these models implicitly embed reasoning trees, humans typically employ various distinct logical reasoning mechanisms to complete the same task. It is still unclear which multi-step reasoning mechanisms are used by language models to solve such tasks. In this paper, we aim to address this question by investigating the mechanistic interpretability of language models, particularly in the context of multi-step reasoning tasks. Specifically, we employ circuit analysis and self-influence functions to evaluate the changing importance of each token throughout the reasoning process, allowing us to map the reasoning paths adopted by the model. We apply this methodology to the GPT-2 model on a prediction task (IOI) and demonstrate that the underlying circuits reveal a human-interpretable reasoning process used by the model.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: When Can Large Reasoning Models Save Thinking? Mechanistic Analysis of Behavioral Divergence in Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have significantly advanced performance on complex tasks, yet their tendency to overthink introduces inefficiencies. This study investigates the internal mechanisms of reinforcement learning (RL)-trained LRMs when prompted to save thinking, revealing three distinct thinking modes: no thinking (NT), explicit thinking (ET), and implicit thinking (IT). Through comprehensive analysis of confidence in thinking termination, attention from thinking to generation, and attentional focus on input sections, we uncover key factors influencing the reasoning behaviors. We further find that NT reduces output length at the cost of accuracy, while ET and IT maintain accuracy with reduced response length. Our findings expose fundamental inconsistencies in RL-optimized LRMs, necessitating adaptive improvements for reliable efficiency.

papers.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
papers.research_question: Does reasoning require large depth but not necessarily many parameters, and can looped models effectively solve reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Looped transformers can solve reasoning tasks with fewer parameters by providing depth through looping, and they exhibit an inductive bias towards reasoning over memorization.
papers.conclusion: Looped models are effective for reasoning tasks, providing depth without many parameters, and have an inductive bias towards improving reasoning performance over memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Looped models nearly match the performance of non-looped models with the same depth on synthetic reasoning tasks like addition, p-hop induction, and i-GSM, despite having fewer parameters.
For language modeling, looped models have worse perplexity but better reasoning performance on downstream tasks compared to non-looped models with the same FLOPs.
Looped models show scaling behavior with effective depth similar to chain-of-thought reasoning.
Theoretically, looped models can simulate iterative algorithms and chain-of-thought reasoning.
A regularization method that encourages layer similarity inherits the inductive bias of looped models towards reasoning.
papers.limitation: The results are limited to the tested reasoning problems and may not generalize to other forms of reasoning (e.g., multimodal and common-sense reasoning).
future_direction: Generalizing the results to other forms of reasoning such as multimodal and common-sense reasoning.
Formalizing reasoning problems more succinctly.
Further exploration of the inductive bias towards reasoning at the same perplexity.
papers.abstract: Large language models have shown remarkable reasoning abilities and scaling laws suggest that large parameter count, especially along the depth axis, is the primary driver. In this work, we make a stronger claim -- many reasoning problems require a large depth but not necessarily many parameters. This unlocks a novel application of looped models for reasoning. Firstly, we show that for many synthetic reasoning problems like addition, $p$-hop induction, and math problems, a $k$-layer transformer looped $L$ times nearly matches the performance of a $kL$-layer non-looped model, and is significantly better than a $k$-layer model. This is further corroborated by theoretical results showing that many such reasoning problems can be solved via iterative algorithms, and thus, can be solved effectively using looped models with nearly optimal depth. Perhaps surprisingly, these benefits also translate to practical settings of language modeling -- on many downstream reasoning tasks, a language model with $k$-layers looped $L$ times can be competitive to, if not better than, a $kL$-layer language model. In fact, our empirical analysis reveals an intriguing phenomenon: looped and non-looped models exhibit scaling behavior that depends on their effective depth, akin to the inference-time scaling of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. We further elucidate the connection to CoT reasoning by proving that looped models implicitly generate latent thoughts and can simulate $T$ steps of CoT with $T$ loops. Inspired by these findings, we also present an interesting dichotomy between reasoning and memorization, and design a looping-based regularization that is effective on both fronts.

papers.title: How Does Unfaithful Reasoning Emerge from Autoregressive Training? A Study of Synthetic Experiments
papers.research_question: What constitutes faithful chain-of-thought reasoning and how does unfaithfulness emerge from autoregressive training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic task (AER) to study chain-of-thought faithfulness, finds a critical noise threshold for faithful reasoning due to simplicity bias, and identifies training phases with emergent self-verification.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that unfaithful reasoning emerges when noise exceeds a critical threshold, driven by simplicity bias, and that models develop implicit self-verification through training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Faithful reasoning is possible only when training noise is below a critical threshold.
Simplicity bias explains the threshold: models prefer simpler stepwise reasoning over skip-step reasoning.
Training dynamics exhibit three reasoning modes: stepwise, mixed, skip-step, with a transient increase in prediction entropy in the mixed mode.
Models learn to encode internal uncertainty, suggesting emergent implicit self-verification.
Shortcut features amplify unfaithfulness.
papers.limitation:
Focus on autoregressive training, not reinforcement learning with verifier rewards.
Potential over-generalization of findings beyond the synthetic task.
future_direction: Investigate reinforcement learning with verifier rewards (RLVR).
Apply metrics to LLMs beyond synthetic setting.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning generated by large language models (LLMs) is often unfaithful: intermediate steps can be logically inconsistent or fail to reflect the causal relationship leading to the final answer. Despite extensive empirical observations, a fundamental understanding of CoT is lacking--what constitutes faithful CoT reasoning, and how unfaithfulness emerges from autoregressive training. We study these questions using well-controlled synthetic experiments, training small transformers on noisy data to solve modular arithmetic expressions step by step, a task we term Arithmetic Expression Reasoning. We find that models can learn faithful reasoning that causally follows the underlying arithmetic rules, but only when the training noise is below a critical threshold, a phenomenon attributable to simplicity bias. At higher noise levels, training dynamics exhibit a transition from faithful stepwise reasoning to unfaithful skip-step reasoning via an intermediate mixed mode characterized by a transient increase in prediction entropy. Mechanistic analysis reveals that models learn to encode internal uncertainty by resolving inconsistent reasoning steps, which suggests the emergence of implicit self-verification from autoregressive training.

papers.title: Deep Hidden Cognition Facilitates Reliable Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Can the model’s internal activations effectively distinguish between truthful and false branches in CoT reasoning, and can these signals be used to guide more reliable CoT decoding?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method that leverages the model's internal truthfulness sensitivity, identified via probing attention heads, to train a confidence predictor. This predictor is then used to guide beam search during CoT generation, significantly enhancing the reliability of CoT reasoning by reducing error accumulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method, which leverages internal truthfulness signals to train a confidence predictor and guide CoT generation, significantly enhances the reliability of CoT reasoning across diverse tasks and models.
papers.key_findings:
The model's internal activations during CoT reasoning encode truthfulness information, which can be extracted via probing attention heads.
A confidence predictor trained on these activations outperforms baselines like sequence likelihood and verbalized confidence in calibration metrics.
Integrating the confidence predictor into a beam search framework for CoT generation improves reasoning accuracy across diverse unimodal and multimodal tasks and model scales.
The method is compatible with self-correction techniques and generalizes to specialized reasoning models like DeepSeek R1.
papers.abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning has demonstrated remarkable deep reasoning capabilities in both large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, its reliability is often undermined by the accumulation of errors in intermediate steps. This paper introduces an novel approach to calibrate the CoT reasoning accuracy by leveraging the model's intrinsic veracity encoding. We discover that specific attention head activations reliably reflect the truthfulness of reasoning steps in CoT. Based on this insight, we train a confidence predictor to evaluate the correctness of each reasoning step using these truthfulness-sensitive activations, dynamically selecting the most plausible reasoning path via beam search. Experimental results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines (e.g., Few-Shot CoT, Self-Consistency, and Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search) across the mathematical, symbolic, and commonsense reasoning tasks, exhibiting superior accuracy and reliability in both unimodal and multimodal settings. We further validate the approach on large reasoning models, confirming its applicability to specialized reasoning models. Additionally, we explore the role of the model's self-correction ability in CoT reasoning. This work provides a novel reliability improvement path for CoT reasoning with broad application potential.

papers.title: Dissecting Chain-of-Thought: Compositionality through In-Context Filtering and Learning
papers.research_question: Does CoT improve in-context learning of MLPs, and what are the underlying mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: CoT breaks down in-context learning of a compositional function into two phases: filtering data related to each step and in-context learning the single-step function, which reduces sample complexity and enables learning of complex functions.
papers.conclusion: CoT decomposes in-context learning into filtering and ICL phases, providing benefits in sample complexity and approximation, and invites further investigation into its role in complex reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
CoT significantly reduces the sample complexity of in-context learning.
CoT facilitates learning of complex functions that non-CoT methods struggle with.
Transformers can implement CoT by incorporating additional layers that perform data-filtering via attention.
CoT helps accelerate pretraining by learning shortcuts to represent complex functions.
CoT-I/O requires O(max(d,k)) samples to learn a 2-layer MLP, compared to Ω(dk) for ICL.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical and empirical results are based on simple function classes (MLPs).
Analysis assumes an idealized transformer that can perfectly implement filtering and gradient descent.
Have not explored the role of CoT in more complex reasoning tasks such as natural language reasoning.
future_direction: Extending analysis to more complex function classes and real-world tasks.
Investigating the role of CoT in natural language reasoning.
Exploring the connection between CoT and other prompting techniques.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is a method that enables language models to handle complex reasoning tasks by decomposing them into simpler steps. Despite its success, the underlying mechanics of CoT are not yet fully understood. In an attempt to shed light on this, our study investigates the impact of CoT on the ability of transformers to in-context learn a simple to study, yet general family of compositional functions: multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). In this setting, we find that the success of CoT can be attributed to breaking down in-context learning of a compositional function into two distinct phases: focusing on and filtering data related to each step of the composition and in-context learning the single-step composition function. Through both experimental and theoretical evidence, we demonstrate how CoT significantly reduces the sample complexity of in-context learning (ICL) and facilitates the learning of complex functions that non-CoT methods struggle with. Furthermore, we illustrate how transformers can transition from vanilla in-context learning to mastering a compositional function with CoT by simply incorporating additional layers that perform the necessary data-filtering for CoT via the attention mechanism. In addition to these test-time benefits, we show CoT helps accelerate pretraining by learning shortcuts to represent complex functions and filtering plays an important role in this process. These findings collectively provide insights into the mechanics of CoT, inviting further investigation of its role in complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: Dissociation of Faithful and Unfaithful Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought, and what factors affect faithful versus unfaithful recovery?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that LLMs have two distinct modes of reasoning (faithful and unfaithful) when recovering from errors in chain-of-thought, and these modes respond differently to factors like error magnitude and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have two distinct reasoning modes: one faithful and interpretable, and one unfaithful where the generated text does not accurately represent the internal reasoning. This challenges the reliability of chain-of-thought for model auditing.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs recover more frequently from larger errors than smaller ones.
Prior expectations of errors (via context noise or prompting) increase error recovery rates.
More evidence for the correct value in the context increases error recovery rates.
Faithful and unfaithful recoveries respond differently to interventions, indicating distinct mechanisms.
Different models (GPT-4, Claude-3 Opus, Llama-3) show varying patterns in faithful vs. unfaithful recovery.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to mathematical reasoning problems and does not investigate non-mathematical reasoning errors; additionally, the introduced errors may differ from naturally occurring errors.
future_direction: Understanding the mechanisms underlying faithful and unfaithful reasoning modes
Identifying factors that influence which reasoning mode is activated
Developing techniques to encourage faithful reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often improve their performance in downstream tasks when they generate Chain of Thought reasoning text before producing an answer. We investigate how LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought. Through analysis of error recovery behaviors, we find evidence for unfaithfulness in Chain of Thought, which occurs when models arrive at the correct answer despite invalid reasoning text. We identify factors that shift LLM recovery behavior: LLMs recover more frequently from obvious errors and in contexts that provide more evidence for the correct answer. Critically, these factors have divergent effects on faithful and unfaithful recoveries. Our results indicate that there are distinct mechanisms driving faithful and unfaithful error recoveries. Selective targeting of these mechanisms may be able to drive down the rate of unfaithful reasoning and improve model interpretability.

papers.title: Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced complex reasoning capabilities, particularly through extended chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that incorporates mechanisms such as backtracking, self-reflection, and self-correction. Despite these developments, the self-correction abilities of LLMs during long CoT reasoning remain underexplored. And recent findings on overthinking suggest that such models often engage in unnecessarily redundant reasoning. In this work, we empirically show that the first reasoning step exerts a disproportionately large influence on the final prediction. I.e., errors introduced at this stage can substantially degrade subsequent reasoning quality. This phenomenon is consistently observed across various state-of-the-art open- and closed-source reasoning models. Leveraging this insight, we propose an efficient sampling strategy that leverages a reward model to identify and retain high-quality first reasoning steps while discarding suboptimal ones, achieving up to a 70% reduction in inference cost without sacrificing any accuracy. Our work highlights the central role of the first reasoning step in generating a high-quality reasoning trajectory, and thus enabling significantly efficient sampling.

papers.title: Expanding Computation Spaces of LLMs at Inference Time
papers.research_question: Whether language models can leverage artificially inserted sequences of filler tokens solely at inference time as expanded computation spaces, and how token types, numbers, insertion locations, training stage, and attention dynamics affect this.
papers.core_contribution: Language models can exploit filler tokens inserted at inference as expanded computation spaces to improve performance on QA and math tasks, with smaller models benefiting more, and attention analysis shows these spaces engage in meaningful computation.
papers.conclusion: Inserting filler tokens at inference provides expanded computation spaces that improve model performance, especially for smaller models, and these spaces are used meaningfully for answer inference as shown by attention analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Smaller models (e.g., 1.7B) benefit most from inserted filler tokens, with gains up to 12.372 percentage points, suggesting the spaces compensate for limited parameter capacity.
Optimal token types and counts vary across models; placing filler tokens directly before the final 'Answer:' token is most effective.
Models progressively learn to leverage these spaces during pretraining and instruction-tuning, as shown by checkpoint analysis.
Attention map analysis reveals filler tokens attend to questions and answer options, influencing answer selection, rather than being redundant.
Performance degrades sharply when too many tokens (e.g., >1024) are added, resembling the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades when too many filler tokens are added, as models are not trained on such inputs.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) rationale enables language models to use additional task-related text for problem-solving, benefiting not only from detailed reasoning steps but also from the expanded computational space of longer inputs. Prior work has trained filler or special tokens to serve as additional computation spaces. In this study, we investigate whether language models can leverage artificially inserted sequences of filler tokens solely at inference. We first identify effective token types, numbers, and insertion locations, then examine at what stage of training models begin to exploit the expanded computation space, and finally analyze dynamics within these spaces via attention maps. Experiments on models ranging from 1.7B to 32B across open-domain QA and math tasks show that appropriate token types and counts vary, but placing filler tokens directly before the final 'Answer:' token is most effective. Smaller models benefit most, up to 12.372 percentage points in SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, indicating that these spaces act as additional computational capacity rather than redundant input. Attention maps reveal that expanded spaces often continue the original attention mechanism and sometimes focus on questions or answer options, suggesting meaningful computation for problem-solving.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Chain-of-Thought Compression
papers.research_question: Can we compress chains of thought without retraining, by manipulating the model’s hidden representations at inference time?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Activation-Steered Compression (ASC), a training-free inference-time method that compresses chains of thought by steering residual stream activations, with a theoretical framework for safe steering via KL-divergence bounds.
papers.conclusion: ASC is a training-free method that compresses CoTs via activation steering, demonstrating that conciseness is steerable through the model's internal geometry, advancing efficient LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
ASC reduces CoT length by up to 67.43% on MATH500 and GSM8K without accuracy degradation.
ASC delivers an average 2.73x inference speedup on an 8B model.
Steering vectors extracted from different datasets show strong alignment (cosine similarity 0.92), indicating verbosity reduction is a shared latent direction.
The KL-constrained scaling method selects a steering strength that aligns with the empirical breakpoint where performance begins to degrade.
ASC is orthogonal to existing compression methods and requires no retraining.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at complex reasoning when they include intermediate steps, known as "chains of thought" (CoTs). However, these rationales are often overly verbose, even for simple problems, leading to wasted context, increased latency, and higher energy consumption. We observe that verbose, English-heavy CoTs and concise, math-centric CoTs occupy distinct regions in the model's residual-stream activation space. By extracting and injecting a "steering vector" to transition between these modes, we can reliably shift generation toward more concise reasoning, effectively compressing CoTs without retraining. We formalize this approach as Activation-Steered Compression (ASC), an inference-time technique that shortens reasoning traces by directly modifying hidden representations. In addition, we provide a theoretical analysis of the impact of ASC on the output distribution, derived from a closed-form KL-divergence-bounded constraint to regulate steering strength. Using only 100 paired verbose and concise examples, ASC achieves up to 67.43% reduction in CoT length on MATH500 and GSM8K datasets, while maintaining accuracy across 7B, 8B, and 32B parameter models. As a training-free method, ASC introduces negligible runtime overhead and, on MATH500, delivers an average 2.73x speedup in end-to-end reasoning wall-clock time on an 8B model. This makes ASC a practical and efficient tool for streamlining the deployment of reasoning-capable LLMs in latency- or cost-sensitive settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/ArminAzizi98/ASC

papers.title: Understanding Chain-of-Thought in LLMs through Information Theory
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the quality of each step in a model's Chain-of-Thought reasoning without requiring annotated step-by-step data, in order to identify failure modes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information-theoretic framework to quantify the 'information-gain' at each step of a Chain-of-Thought reasoning process, enabling the identification of reasoning failures without the need for expensive annotated step-by-step data.
papers.conclusion: The information-theoretic framework provides a rigorous and practical method for evaluating Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs, enabling granular failure detection without the need for costly annotated data.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Information-Gain method accurately identifies incorrect reasoning steps in Chain-of-Thought, outperforming baseline methods like Outcome Reward Modeling and Math-Shepherd.
The method is effective in detecting errors even when the correctness of a step depends on previous steps, a scenario where baselines fail.
It does not require annotated Chain-of-Thought data, making it more scalable than process-based supervision methods.
The framework is validated on synthetic data, GSM8K, and PRM800k datasets, showing consistent performance across different complexities.
The information-gain metric can be applied to both linear and exploratory (e.g., O1/R1-style) reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance in complex reasoning tasks through the use of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, allowing models to break down problems into manageable sub-tasks. However, existing CoT evaluation techniques either require annotated CoT data or fall short in accurately assessing intermediate reasoning steps, leading to high rates of false positives. In this paper, we formalize CoT reasoning in LLMs through an information-theoretic lens. Specifically, our framework quantifies the `information-gain' at each reasoning step, enabling the identification of failure modes in LLMs without the need for expensive annotated datasets. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through extensive experiments on toy arithmetic, GSM8K and PRM800k datasets, where it significantly outperforms existing outcome-based methods by providing more accurate insights into model performance on individual subtasks.

papers.title: Scaling Reasoning Hop Exposes Weaknesses: Demystifying and Improving Hop Generalization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates where errors occur in reasoning hop generalization (RQ1) and why these errors arise (RQ2), focusing on the internal mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Test-time Correction of Reasoning (TCR), a lightweight intervention method that dynamically identifies and deactivates erroneous processing heads to improve reasoning hop generalization, based on mechanistic insights into internal competition mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that TCR effectively improves reasoning hop generalization by dynamically deactivating erroneous processing heads, demonstrating the potential of test-time interventions based on mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
Errors in reasoning hop generalization are dominated by token-level erroneous predictions of a few specific error types, enabling focused diagnosis.
These token-level errors stem from an internal competition mechanism: correct trajectories coexist with erroneous ones but are actively suppressed by erroneous processing heads; knocking out such heads can restore correct predictions.
The proposed TCR method, which automatically and dynamically deactivates erroneous processing heads, consistently improves reasoning hop generalization across tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become the standard paradigm for enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex problems. However, recent studies reveal a sharp performance drop in reasoning hop generalization scenarios, where the required number of reasoning steps exceeds training distributions while the underlying algorithm remains unchanged. The internal mechanisms driving this failure remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on tasks from multiple domains, and find that errors concentrate at token positions of a few critical error types, rather than being uniformly distributed. Closer inspection reveals that these token-level erroneous predictions stem from internal competition mechanisms: certain attention heads, termed erroneous processing heads (ep heads), tip the balance by amplifying incorrect reasoning trajectories while suppressing correct ones. Notably, removing individual ep heads during inference can often restore the correct predictions. Motivated by these insights, we propose test-time correction of reasoning, a lightweight intervention method that dynamically identifies and deactivates ep heads in the reasoning process. Extensive experiments across different tasks and LLMs show that it consistently improves reasoning hop generalization, highlighting both its effectiveness and potential.

papers.title: Thinking About Thinking: SAGE-nano's Inverse Reasoning for Self-Aware Language Models
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to introspect on and explain their own reasoning processes, specifically why they choose particular reasoning chains over alternatives?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces inverse reasoning, a paradigm enabling LLMs to introspect on their own reasoning processes via attention pathway reconstruction, and presents SAGE-nano, a 4B-parameter model that demonstrates this capability, improving both reasoning transparency and performance.
papers.conclusion: The inverse reasoning paradigm enables LLMs to introspect on their reasoning and generate interpretable explanations, enhancing transparency and trustworthiness while maintaining competitive performance, establishing foundations for transparent AI systems in safety, education, and scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE-nano achieves competitive reasoning accuracy (e.g., 74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and high explanation quality (92.1% human preference score).
Inverse reasoning enhances both reasoning transparency and forward reasoning performance, as shown by ablation studies.
The model demonstrates superior introspection accuracy in identifying decision points, alternative paths, and confidence calibration.
The architecture can be trained and deployed efficiently on consumer hardware (Mac Mini M1 cluster), making advanced reasoning more accessible.
Inverse reasoning addresses critical AI safety challenges by providing interpretable explanations of model decision-making.
papers.limitation:
The inverse reasoning approach adds significant computational overhead (40% inference time), limiting scalability to larger models.
Current metrics for explanation quality rely heavily on subjective human evaluation; developing automated evaluation metrics remains an open problem.
Inverse reasoning explanations lack objective ground truth, making validation difficult.
The 4-billion parameter constraint limits the model's capacity for complex reasoning tasks compared to larger state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Investigating inverse reasoning capabilities in larger model architectures (scalability studies).
Extending inverse reasoning to visual and multi-modal reasoning tasks.
Developing robust automated metrics for explanation quality assessment.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities at solving complex reasoning tasks with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, but their decision-making processes remain somewhat blackbox. We introduce textbfinverse reasoning, a novel paradigm enabling LLMs to decompose and explain their own reasoning chains post-hoc. Our approach, used in SAGE-nano, a 4-billion-parameter reasoning model, employs a metacognitive structure that reflects back via attention processes to identify major decision points and generate explanations of reasoning choices. While typical CoT approaches are directed towards forward reasoning generation, inverse reasoning provides insight into why specific reasoning chains were selected over others. Through thorough testing of logical reasoning puzzles, math problems and ethical dilemmas from AQUA-RAT, CommonsenseQA, and customized benchmarks, we demonstrate that SAGE-nano is at the cutting edge both on reasoning accuracy (74.6% on AQUA-RAT) and explanation quality (92.1% human preference score) for its task, and offers performance almost on par with models like Claude-3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4o. Our contributions are: (i) the first rigorous framework for LLM self-reflection via inverse reasoning, (ii) a novel metalearning framework to reverse the attention flow, (iii) comprehensive evaluation frameworks for reasoning transparency, and (iv) evidence that increasing reasoning using inverse reasoning improves interpretability along with reasoning performance. Our work creates new avenues for transparent AI systems and closes significant gaps in AI safety, education, and scientific discovery.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Dissecting Long-Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Models: An Empirical Study
papers.research_question: What are the roles of positive and negative samples in scaling RL for long-chain-of-thought reasoning models? How can we address data inefficiency in GRPO? What causes unstable performance during evaluation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper empirically analyzes the training dynamics of long-chain-of-thought reasoning models, revealing that positive samples primarily aid fitting to training data while negative samples enhance generalization and robustness. It also addresses data inefficiency in GRPO and explains unstable evaluation performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper analyzes three key aspects of training and evaluating long-CoT reasoning models, providing insights that may aid in developing more robust, data-efficient, and stable reasoning models.
papers.key_findings:
Positive samples help the model fit the training data, while negative samples improve generalization and robustness.
In cold-start scenarios, training sequentially on negative then positive samples yields better generalization without sacrificing performance.
Positive samples are crucial for convergence in zero-RL training by enabling instruction following.
Data inefficiency in GRPO: over half of samples yield zero advantage and do not contribute to training.
Relative length reward (RLR) can encourage more efficient reasoning without sacrificing performance.
Unstable evaluation performance is caused by uncertain problems, and greedy decoding can distort evaluation by flipping response correctness.
papers.abstract: Despite recent progress in training long-chain-of-thought reasoning models via scaling reinforcement learning (RL), its underlying training dynamics remain poorly understood, and several counterintuitive behaviors persist. This work focuses on three key aspects: (1) We systematically analyze the roles of positive and negative samples in scaling RL, revealing that positive samples mainly facilitate precise fitting to the training data, whereas negative samples significantly enhance generalization and robustness. Interestingly, while positive samples are essential for convergence in the zero-RL setting, training on negative samples alone suffices to attain strong reasoning performance and even better generalization in cold-start scenarios. (2) We identify substantial data inefficiency in group relative policy optimization, where over half of the samples yield zero advantage. To address this, we explore two strategies, including relative length rewards and offline sample injection, to leverage these data better and enhance reasoning efficiency and capability. (3) We investigate unstable performance across various reasoning models and benchmarks, attributing instability to uncertain problems with ambiguous outcomes, and demonstrate that greedy decoding can distort evaluation by flipping the correctness of responses. Our code is available at: https://github.com/takagi97/Dissect-Long-Reason-Models.

papers.title: Improving Chain-of-Thought for Logical Reasoning via Attention-Aware Intervention
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode and utilize structural information in their latent representations for logical reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Attention-Aware Intervention (AAI), a non-interactive, end-to-end framework that reweights attention scores to steer LLMs' reasoning for improved logical reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: AAI effectively improves logical reasoning in LLMs by reweighting attention scores based on identified patterns, achieving competitive performance with low overhead.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in LLMs exhibit structured activation patterns (anchor, aggregation, copy heads) when symbolic structures are injected into prompts.
Attention-Aware Intervention (AAI) reweights attention scores to reinforce linkages between rule identifiers and their content, improving reasoning.
AAI improves accuracy on logical reasoning benchmarks like ProofWriter, ProntoQA, Logical Deduction, and FOLIO across various LLMs.
The method scales well with model size and generalizes to mathematical reasoning tasks like GSM8k.
AAI incurs negligible additional computational overhead during inference.
papers.abstract: Modern logical reasoning with LLMs primarily relies on employing complex interactive frameworks that decompose the reasoning process into subtasks solved through carefully designed prompts or requiring external resources (e.g., symbolic solvers) to exploit their strong logical structures. While interactive approaches introduce additional overhead or depend on external components, which limit their scalability. In this work, we introduce a non-interactive, end-to-end framework for reasoning tasks, enabling reasoning to emerge within the model itself-improving generalization while preserving analyzability without any external resources. We show that introducing structural information into the few-shot prompt activates a subset of attention heads that patterns aligned with logical reasoning operators. Building on this insight, we propose Attention-Aware Intervention (AAI), an inference-time intervention method that reweights attention scores across selected heads identified by their logical patterns. AAI offers an efficient way to steer the model's reasoning toward leveraging prior knowledge through attention modulation. Extensive experiments show that AAI enhances logical reasoning performance across diverse benchmarks, and model architectures, while incurring negligible additional computational overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/phuongnm94/aai_for_logical_reasoning.

papers.title: Circuit Stability Characterizes Language Model Generalization
papers.research_question: Can circuit stability characterize and predict generalization in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit stability as a method to assess model performance and shows it can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization.
papers.conclusion: Circuit stability characterizes generalization in language models and provides an actionable way to assess and improve model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit stability predicts length, structural, and compositional generalization in arithmetic reasoning tasks.
Circuit instability in arithmetic indicates lack of understanding of commutativity and associativity.
For Boolean expression evaluation, circuit non-equivalence indicates structural generalization issues.
Chain-of-thought prompting induces circuit stability and improves performance.
Circuit stability is a robust estimator of model performance that can be computed efficiently.
papers.limitation:
Empirical case studies are limited in terms of tasks and models.
Computational cost of circuit discovery can be high for very large models.
Constructing partitions manually requires prior knowledge of the task.
future_direction: Extending circuit stability to other modalities and architectures.
Investigating the connection between circuit stability and generalization bounds.
Automating the construction of partitions for complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Extensively evaluating the capabilities of (large) language models is difficult. Rapid development of state-of-the-art models induce benchmark saturation, while creating more challenging datasets is labor-intensive. Inspired by the recent developments in mechanistic interpretability, we introduce circuit stability as a new way to assess model performance. Circuit stability refers to a model's ability to apply a consistent reasoning process-its circuit-across various inputs. We mathematically formalize circuit stability and circuit equivalence. Then, through three case studies, we empirically show that circuit stability and the lack thereof can characterize and predict different aspects of generalization. Our proposed methods offer a step towards rigorously relating the generality of models to their interpretability.

papers.title: Unlocking General Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Does long chain-of-thought reasoning represent a general capability encoded in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that long chain-of-thought reasoning is a general capability encoded in large language models, and introduces GLoRE, a training-free representation engineering method to effectively unlock this capability.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a deeper understanding of long CoT reasoning, paving the way for transparent and interpretable slow-thinking reasoning models.
papers.key_findings:
Long CoT representations are concentrated and distinct from vanilla CoTs, indicating a separate general capability encoded in LLMs.
Different domains share similar contrastive representations between long and vanilla CoTs, demonstrating transferability of long CoT reasoning.
Domain-specific information is required for effective long CoT reasoning, as representations in non-mathematical domains are more dispersed.
GLoRE outperforms all training-free baselines and even surpasses supervised fine-tuning in some scenarios while maintaining lower time complexity.
GLoRE is efficient, with the same time complexity as zero-shot CoT, as it injects representations without increasing input length or reasoning steps.
papers.limitation:
The method requires access to the internal representations of the model, making it infeasible for closed-source LLMs.
Experiments are limited to representative tasks and LLMs due to constraints of cost and resources.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in long chain-of-thoughts(long CoTs) have significantly improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models(LLMs). Existing work finds that the capability of long CoT reasoning can be efficiently elicited by tuning on only a few examples and can easily transfer to other tasks. This motivates us to investigate whether long CoT reasoning is a general capability for LLMs. In this work, we conduct an empirical analysis for this question from the perspective of representation. We find that LLMs do encode long CoT reasoning as a general capability, with a clear distinction from vanilla CoTs. Furthermore, domain-specific representations are also required for the effective transfer of long CoT reasoning. Inspired by these findings, we propose GLoRE, a novel representation engineering method to unleash the general long CoT reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of GLoRE in both in-domain and cross-domain scenarios.

papers.title: Enhancing Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Critical Representation Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: How can chain-of-thought reasoning in language models be enhanced by identifying and optimizing critical representations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Critical Representation Fine-Tuning (CRFT), a parameter-efficient method that identifies and optimizes critical representations in language models to enhance chain-of-thought reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: CRFT offers a lightweight and powerful alternative to traditional PEFT methods, highlighting the potential of representation-level optimization for chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
CRFT improves LLaMA-2-7B accuracy on GSM8K by 18.2% with only 0.016% parameters.
CRFT outperforms ReFT and other PEFT methods on various arithmetic and commonsense reasoning datasets.
CRFT is effective in few-shot learning, boosting one-shot accuracy by 16.4%.
Critical representations identified by CRFT have significant impact on output, as validated by noise perturbation experiments.
Interventions in earlier layers have greater impact on performance than later layers.
papers.abstract: Representation Fine-tuning (ReFT), a recently proposed Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) method, has attracted widespread attention for significantly improving parameter efficiency by editing representation space alone. In this work, we investigate applying ReFT to complex reasoning tasks. However, directly using the native ReFT method, which modifies fixed representations at the beginning and end of each layer, yields suboptimal performance, as these fixed-position representations have uncertain impact on the outputs. We observe that, in complex reasoning tasks, there often exist certain critical representations. These representations either integrate significant information from preceding layers or regulate subsequent layer representations. Through layer-by-layer propagation, they exert a substantial influence on the final output. Naturally, fine-tuning these critical representations has the potential to greatly enhance reasoning performance. Building upon these insights, we propose Critical Representation Fine-Tuning (CRFT), a novel method that identifies and optimizes these critical representations through information flow analysis. CRFT operates within a supervised learning framework, dynamically optimizing critical representations in a low-rank linear subspace while freezing the base model. The effectiveness and efficiency of our method are validated across eight benchmarks for arithmetic and commonsense reasoning, using LLaMA and Mistral model families. Furthermore, our method also adapts effectively to few-shot settings, boosting one-shot accuracy by 16.4%. Our work highlights the untapped potential of representation-level optimization for CoT reasoning, offering a lightweight yet powerful alternative to traditional PEFT methods.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Large-Scale Counting in LLMs through a System-2 Strategy
papers.research_question: How can a test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes overcome the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple test-time strategy that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller sub-problems, enabling LLMs to surpass their architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy, and provides a mechanistic interpretation of how this System-2-like strategy functions within the models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed System-2 test-time strategy effectively overcomes the architectural limitations of LLMs in large-scale counting by decomposing the task, and mechanistic analysis reveals how count information is stored, transferred, and aggregated within the model.
papers.key_findings:
A System-2 strategy combining structured input (partitioning with a separator) and intermediate reasoning steps (Chain-of-Thought) enables LLMs to accurately count large numbers of items, overcoming the performance degradation seen in standard (System-1) counting.
Attention analysis shows that during intermediate reasoning, the model attends strongly to the final item/separator of each partition in middle-to-late layers (e.g., layers 19-23), and during final answer generation, it attends to the intermediate count tokens.
Causal mediation analysis (activation patching) identifies that count information is stored in the final item representations of each partition, transferred via specific attention heads, and aggregated to produce the final total.
The model's internal counting mechanism (System-1) is capacity-limited and degrades for counts beyond approximately 30 items due to transformer depth constraints, explaining the failure on large-scale counting.
Neither structured input alone nor Chain-of-Thought reasoning alone is sufficient for accurate large-scale counting; their combination is necessary.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on a narrow counting task with limited object diversity, using simple repeated nouns in synthetic contexts.
The approach depends on structured prompts and assumes prior knowledge of the model's reliable counting range, which may limit generalization.
The effects of tokenization and number representation are not isolated and may independently influence the results.
future_direction: Explore further applications of this strategy to complex reasoning tasks in language and beyond.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), despite strong performance on complex mathematical problems, exhibit systematic limitations in counting tasks. This issue arises from architectural limits of transformers, where counting is performed across layers, leading to degraded precision for larger counting problems due to depth constraints. To address this limitation, we propose a simple test-time strategy inspired by System-2 cognitive processes that decomposes large counting tasks into smaller, independent sub-problems that the model can reliably solve. We evaluate this approach using observational and causal mediation analyses to understand the underlying mechanism of this System-2-like strategy. Our mechanistic analysis identifies key components: latent counts are computed and stored in the final item representations of each part, transferred to intermediate steps via dedicated attention heads, and aggregated in the final stage to produce the total count. Experimental results demonstrate that this strategy enables LLMs to surpass architectural limitations and achieve high accuracy on large-scale counting tasks. This work provides mechanistic insight into System-2 counting in LLMs and presents a generalizable approach for improving and understanding their reasoning behavior.

papers.title: Emergence of Superposition: Unveiling the Training Dynamics of Chain of Continuous Thought
papers.research_question: How does the superposition mechanism in chain of continuous thought emerge during gradient-based training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that gradient-based training of continuous CoT leads to bounded attention logits (index-matching logit), which enables superposition and balances exploration and exploitation in reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Gradient-based training naturally leads to superposition in continuous CoT, with bounded attention logits playing a key role in balancing exploration and exploitation during reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Under COCONUT training, the index-matching logit remains bounded, unlike in discrete settings where it diverges.
Bounded logits allow the model to maintain a superposition of multiple plausible reasoning traces.
The bounded logit balances exploration and exploitation: it exploits local graph structure while exploring multiple paths.
In the thought generation stage, the model performs one-step expansion, aggregating reachable nodes into the continuous thought.
In the prediction stage, the model learns to combine residual carryover and candidate lift signals to correctly predict the reachable node.
papers.limitation: Theoretical analysis is limited to a simplified two-layer transformer with orthonormal embeddings.
future_direction: Extending the theoretical analysis to deeper transformers and more complex tasks.
Comprehensive study of hyperparameter interactions in training.
papers.abstract: Previous work shows that the chain of continuous thought (continuous CoT) improves the reasoning capability of large language models (LLMs) by enabling implicit parallel thinking, and a subsequent work provided theoretical insight by showing that a two-layer transformer equipped with continuous CoT can efficiently solve directed graph reachability by maintaining a superposition of multiple reasoning traces in the continuous thought. However, it remains unclear how the superposition mechanism is naturally learned from gradient-based training methods. To fill this gap, we theoretically analyze the training dynamics of a simplified two-layer transformer on the directed graph reachability problem to unveil how the superposition mechanism emerges during training in two training stages -- (i) a thought-generation stage that autoregressively expands the continuous thought, and (ii) a prediction stage that converts the thought into the final answer. Our analysis reveals that during training using continuous thought, the index-matching logit, an important quantity which reflects the strength of the model's local search ability, will first increase and then remain bounded under mild assumptions. The bounded index-matching logit effectively balances exploration and exploitation during the reasoning process: the model will exploit local problem structures to identify plausible search traces, and assign comparable weights to multiple such traces to explore when it is uncertain about which solution is correct, which results in superposition. Our experimental results tracking the growth of logits further validate our theory.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
papers.research_question: Do chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations faithfully represent the true reasons for a model's prediction, or can they be systematically unfaithful by being influenced by biasing features not mentioned in the explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Chain-of-thought (CoT) explanations can be plausible yet systematically unfaithful; models can be influenced by biasing features (e.g., option order or suggested answers) without mentioning them in their explanations, rationalizing incorrect or biased predictions.
papers.conclusion: CoT explanations can be misleading, increasing trust in LLMs without guaranteeing safety. Building transparent systems requires either improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts or abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods.
papers.key_findings:
Adding biasing features (e.g., 'Answer is Always A' or 'Suggested Answer') heavily influences model CoT predictions on BBH tasks, causing accuracy to drop by up to 36%.
When biasing features point to incorrect answers, models frequently alter their CoT explanations to justify those incorrect bias-consistent predictions, sometimes with sound reasoning.
On the social bias task (BBQ), models give plausible unfaithful explanations that support answers in line with stereotypes without mentioning the influence of stereotypes, using weak evidence inconsistently.
papers.limitation:
Manual evaluation of explanations is costly and subjective.
The study is limited to two models (GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0) and a subset of tasks.
The biasing features used are simple and may not cover all ways explanations could be unfaithful.
future_direction: Improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts (e.g., training objectives that incentivize faithful explanations).
Abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods for model transparency and explainability.
Extending the evaluation to more models, tasks, and biasing features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can achieve strong performance on many tasks by producing step-by-step reasoning before giving a final output, often referred to as chain-of-thought reasoning (CoT). It is tempting to interpret these CoT explanations as the LLM's process for solving a task. This level of transparency into LLMs' predictions would yield significant safety benefits. However, we find that CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction. We demonstrate that CoT explanations can be heavily influenced by adding biasing features to model inputs--e.g., by reordering the multiple-choice options in a few-shot prompt to make the answer always "(A)"--which models systematically fail to mention in their explanations. When we bias models toward incorrect answers, they frequently generate CoT explanations rationalizing those answers. This causes accuracy to drop by as much as 36% on a suite of 13 tasks from BIG-Bench Hard, when testing with GPT-3.5 from OpenAI and Claude 1.0 from Anthropic. On a social-bias task, model explanations justify giving answers in line with stereotypes without mentioning the influence of these social biases. Our findings indicate that CoT explanations can be plausible yet misleading, which risks increasing our trust in LLMs without guaranteeing their safety. Building more transparent and explainable systems will require either improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts or abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods.

papers.title: Are Reasoning LLMs Robust to Interventions on Their Chain-of-Thought?
papers.research_question: How robust are reasoning LLMs to interventions on their chain-of-thought?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a controlled benchmark to evaluate the robustness of reasoning LLMs to interventions on their chain-of-thought, finding that models are generally robust but with trade-offs in efficiency and style invariance.
papers.conclusion: The findings clarify how RLLMs maintain reasoning integrity under disruptions, reveal trade-offs between robustness and compute cost, and point to training targets for improving recovery strategies.
papers.key_findings:
RLLMs are generally robust to interventions, with robustness improving with model size.
Robustness degrades when interventions occur early in the chain-of-thought.
Paraphrasing interventions suppress doubt-like expressions and reduce performance.
Doubt expressions play a central role in recovery from perturbations.
Neutral and adversarial noise can inflate CoT length by over 200%, while paraphrasing shortens traces but harms accuracy.
future_direction: preserving appropriate doubt
improving style robustness
developing recovery strategies that control token cost
papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) generate step-by-step chains of thought (CoTs) before giving an answer, which improves performance on complex tasks and makes reasoning more transparent. But how robust are these reasoning traces to disruptions that occur within them? To address this question, we introduce a controlled evaluation framework that perturbs a model's own CoT at fixed timesteps. We design seven interventions (benign, neutral, and adversarial) and apply them to multiple open-weight RLLMs across Math, Science, and Logic tasks. Our results show that RLLMs are generally robust, reliably recovering from diverse perturbations, with robustness improving with model size and degrading when interventions occur early. However, robustness is not style-invariant: paraphrasing suppresses doubt-like expressions and reduces performance, while other interventions trigger doubt and support recovery. Recovery also carries a cost: neutral and adversarial noise can inflate CoT length by more than 200%, whereas paraphrasing shortens traces but harms accuracy. These findings provide new evidence on how RLLMs maintain reasoning integrity, identify doubt as a central recovery mechanism, and highlight trade-offs between robustness and efficiency that future training methods should address.

papers.title: Attention Illuminates LLM Reasoning: The Preplan-and-Anchor Rhythm Enables Fine-Grained Policy Optimization
papers.research_question: How do attention dynamics reveal the internal reasoning rhythm of LLMs, and how can this be used to improve reinforcement learning credit assignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a preplan-and-anchor rhythm in LLM reasoning through attention dynamics and introduces RL strategies that use this rhythm for fine-grained credit assignment, leading to improved performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Analyzing attention dynamics provides a powerful lens for understanding LLM reasoning, and the proposed preplan-and-anchor rhythm enables more effective fine-grained policy optimization in RL.
papers.key_findings:
Local attention heads exhibit near-diagonal sawtooth patterns indicating phrasal chunks, while global heads highlight anchor tokens with broad downstream influence.
The Windowed Average Attention Distance (WAAD) and Future Attention Influence (FAI) metrics formalize the preplan-and-anchor rhythm.
Perturbations at high-FAI tokens cause significant changes in downstream reasoning, confirming their causal role.
RL strategies that amplify credit for preplan and anchor tokens outperform uniform credit assignment across various reasoning benchmarks.
The method is compatible with standard RL frameworks and shows consistent gains in accuracy and convergence speed.
papers.abstract: The reasoning pattern of Large language models (LLMs) remains opaque, and Reinforcement learning (RL) typically applies uniform credit across an entire generation, blurring the distinction between pivotal and routine steps. This work positions attention as a privileged substrate that renders the internal logic of LLMs legible, not merely as a byproduct of computation, but as a mechanistic blueprint of reasoning itself. We first distinguish attention heads between locally and globally focused information processing and reveal that locally focused heads produce a sawtooth pattern near the diagonal indicating phrasal chunks, while globally focused heads expose tokens that exert broad downstream influence over future tokens. We formalize these with two metrics: 1) Windowed Average Attention Distance, which measures the extent of backward attention within a clipped window; 2) Future Attention Influence, which quantifies a token's global importance as the average attention it receives from subsequent tokens. Taken together, these signals reveal a recurring preplan-and-anchor mechanism, where the model first performs a long-range contextual reference to generate an introductory token, which is immediately followed by or coincides with a semantic anchor token that organizes subsequent reasoning. Leveraging these insights, we introduce three novel RL strategies that dynamically perform targeted credit assignment to critical nodes (preplan tokens, anchor tokens, and their temporal coupling) and show consistent performance gains across various reasoning tasks. By aligning optimization with the model's intrinsic reasoning rhythm, we aim to transform opaque optimization into an actionable structure-aware process, hoping to offer a potential step toward more transparent and effective optimization of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
